records.name: Gideon
records.held_by: The Gideon civic council in the old Governor's Mansion, over a Lukiul Argonian majority with Nibenese-descended families
records.summary: Gideon is the western frontier city of Black Marsh, built on the one dry road through a flooded hillscape and on the Ayleid ruins of Twyllbek. In 4E 201 it keeps a working courthouse, records and a civic council, and openly denies the legitimacy of the Archwardens' successor state.

notes.text: Gideon is the first settlement on the Blackwood Road from Leyawiin and the province's civic-and-records city: a governor's mansion, a courthouse, a Temple of Dibella, an arena and mud bathhouses in a labyrinth of cramped streets. Most buildings stand along Blackwood Way because it is the only dry ground through the town.

Barsaebic Ayleids founded it as Twyllbek; the Kothringi left a Dibella devotion in the soil; Imperial settlers built the mansion, the temple and Castle Giovesse beside it. The An-Xileel's weapon killed the Lukiul majority in 4E 48 and the undead host of Umbriel overran the town, yet Gideon's destruction was light and it stayed an active settlement.

In 4E 201 the council still sits in the Governor's Mansion and the courthouse still hears cases, because Gideon is the one place with a paper tradition to keep. The town denies the successor state's claim over it and trades with the Archwardens only for what it must, while the Blackwood Road to Leyawiin carries traffic whenever the monsoon allows.

Majority Lukiul Argonians who speak Cyrodiilic, do business quietly and lean away from Argonian philosophy, beside Nibenese-descended families two centuries settled. Archein families survive as landholders and clerks. About 90 people live in the walls; Khajiit and Bosmer traders pass through.

Hunting produce, herbs, red-clay pottery from the Onkobra delta, and the Leyawiin trade; the cooks serve outsiders the swamp food they can stomach. The rootworm's winter terminus brings Middle Argonian goods, and salt and iron go out to the river stations of the Naka-Desh.

Dibella is worshipped openly in the old Dorcia Martius manor, a devotion the Nibenese took from the Kothringi substrate; Sithis is honoured quietly by the Argonians. The Hist garden holds a planted cutting whose ownership is disputed.

Imperial brick and timber along Blackwood Way, wet red clay underfoot, crooked alleys running off the causeway, and Ayleid white-stone stumps in the plaza and the southern gardens. Steam rises from the bathhouses and fog lies in the streets at dawn.
The town is guarded and safe by day. The closed Ayleid sections, the Ruction Ring's cut-throats and the swamp at the gates (death hoppers, fleshflies, hackwings) are where visitors get hurt.
A courthouse case that turns on a missing record, the disputed Hist cutting in the gardens, the closed Ayleid cellars, digs for Kothringi treasure and the Gideon-Soulrest rivalry all start here.

notes.text: Calyphe was a Dibella shrine of the Kothringi at the western end of the mangrove country, a few miles from the Gideon road. When the Knahaten Flu emptied the Blackwood in 2E 560 its keepers died untended, and the mangroves have grown through the floor since.
The shrine is unheld. Diggers from Gideon reach it by flat-bottomed boat through the mangrove channels, and Naka-Desh boatmen tie a chime to the roots at the landing on their way past.
No one lives here. A Nibenese shrine-seeker from Gideon may leave an offering at the altar slab, and the diggers keep a camp on the one dry hummock beside it.
It was a place of offerings, not of trade. Now the leaf-carved stone is prised out and carried to Gideon, and small gold and silver votives are still turned up in the root-mud.

The altar slab is Dibella's, and the leaf-and-wave carving on it is the Kothringi sign of her. Gideon's Nibenese bring flowers and wine to it, and the Naka-Desh hang tin chimes in the mangroves above.
Leaf-carved grey stone sunk to the lintels in black mud, with mangrove roots arched over the altar and the broken pillars. Chimes tick in the branches over it.
Mangrove crocodiles and mudcrabs lie in the channel at the landing, and the footing around the altar gives way under a heavy boot. Ghost lights at dusk are said to draw the careless into the pools.
A buried offering-vault, a chime-keeper who guards the roots, or a Gideon digger hunting a Dibella relic.

notes.text: Eurydike was a hall of Kothringi knights who took the Empire's pay as part of Gideon's garrison in the Third Era. After the Flu of 2E 560 the old hall stood empty, and its barracks block fell in during the Oblivion Crisis storms.

notes.text: Mnemosa is a burial terrace of the Kothringi on the high ground of Nha Enasa, east of Gideon. The terrace was filled at the height of the Flu in 2E 560, so the stones carry far more names than the settlement ever had.

No one holds it. The Naka-Desh treat it as a place to be visited, not lived in, and paddle up from the channels to renew their chimes. Diggers who rob the terraces are driven off if the river-folk catch them.
Nobody lives here. Naka-Desh come in pairs at the turn of the year to tend the chime-posts, and now and then a grave-robber from Gideon is found in the reeds.
The terrace was the Kothringi's burial ground, so it never traded. Now it draws grave-robbers after the burial goods, and the Naka-Desh keep it as a place of memory worth more than any grave-gold.

Each grave is marked with a stone and a chime-post, and the Kothringi hung tin and copper chimes there to speak to the dead. The Naka-Desh, friends of the Kothringi in life, keep the ring of posts in repair.
Stepped terraces of grave-stones set in a ring of weathered chime-posts, with the posts hung with green-crusted tin and copper. Reeds have taken the lowest step and a shallow pool sits in the middle.
The dead of the terrace stir at night and the pool is deep with leeches. Naka-Desh watchers will shoot at a looter who disturbs the graves.

notes.text: Pelaxis was the Kothringi river quay and boat-house on the channel east of Gideon, where shallow-draft sail-and-paddle boats were built and repaired. When the Flu emptied it in 2E 560, the last boat was left half-planked on the slip.

notes.text: Dorianth was the longhouse of a seafaring Kothringi family, the sort who sailed the coast and traded up the Nha Enasa channels. The leviathan-horn on its lintel was the family's mark, and no one of the family survived the Flu of 2E 560.
No one holds it. Its lintel stone is the one thing that draws visitors: Paatru and Naka-Desh both know it and use the hall as a shelter against the monsoon.
Nobody lives here. Paatru hunters from the camps to the east use the hall's hearth during the rains, and a Gideon scholar comes now and then to copy the lintel.
